stories.title: I Didn’t Disappear
stories.description: A reflective piece about resilience, identity, and rebuilding after unexpected change. Through moments of silence and uncertainty, the author explores the process of finding oneself again and discovering that even when life pauses, one’s strength and hope can remain.
stories.authorBio: Hasina Rahimy is a young Afghan woman passionate about learning, storytelling, and personal growth. She believes in turning challenges into strength and using her voice to inspire others.  Through writing, she expresses her journey, emotions, and hope for a better future. She is continuously learning and building a meaningful path for herself.
stories.content:
There was a time when my life felt normal. Not perfect, but steady. I had things to do, places to go, and a reason to wake up and keep moving.
  
I didn’t think much about the future. I was just living it.  

Then everything changed.  

The things I used to do stopped. The routines I depended on slowly disappeared. And without warning, my life became very quiet.  

At first, I told myself it wouldn’t last. I thought it was just a pause, something temporary. But days turned into weeks, and nothing went back to how it was before.  

That’s when silence started to feel heavy.  

Not the kind of silence that is peaceful, but the kind that makes you think too much. The kind where you start questioning yourself, your place, your purpose. 
I didn’t know what to do with that feeling.  

Some days I felt stuck. Some days I felt like I was falling behind. And some days I didn’t feel much at all.  

I started noticing how silence changes you. It doesn’t come suddenly. It grows slowly, until even simple things feel difficult. Even your thoughts feel heavier than before.  

But even in that space, something inside me didn’t fully give up. 
 
It was small. Quiet. Not strong enough to call hope, but strong enough to keep me from stopping completely.
  
So I started doing small things again. I tried to bring structure back into my days, even if it was very little. I focused on simple routines, simple goals, simple steps that didn’t feel overwhelming.  

Some days I succeeded. Some days I didn’t. But I kept trying.  

And slowly, I began to understand something important. 
 
I didn’t disappear just because my life changed.  

I didn’t lose myself just because things stopped. 
 
I was still here.  

As Maya Angelou once said, “You may encounter many defeats, but you must not be defeated.” That thought became something I carried with me quietly, especially on the days I felt weakest.  

I realized that life doesn’t always fall apart loudly. Sometimes it just pauses. And in that pause,  you either lose yourself or slowly find yourself again.  

I am still in that process.  

Still learning how to move forward. Still rebuilding parts of myself I thought were gone. Still trying, even when it feels slow. 
 
But now I know something I didn’t know before: 
 
As Viktor E. Frankl said, “When we are no longer able to change a situation, we are  challenged to change ourselves.” And maybe that is what I am doing now.  

I am not sure what happened to me. 
I am what I choose to become after it.  
And I didn’t disappear.

stories.title: The Threads That Carried My Dreams
stories.description: From weaving carpets as a six-year-old to dreaming of becoming a business leader, this inspiring personal narrative tells the story of Freshta, whose resilience transforms hardship into hope. Through perseverance, education, and an unwavering belief in herself, she shows that even the most fragile dreams can be woven into a brighter future.
stories.authorBio: Freshta Nazari is a twelfth-grade student from Afghanistan who has balanced education with work from an early age. She has woven carpets since she was six years old while continuing to pursue her education with determination. Passionate about girls' education, leadership, and entrepreneurship, she hopes to become a business leader who creates opportunities for young women and helps build stronger communities. Through her writing, she shares stories of resilience to inspire others never to give up on their dreams.
stories.content:
Winter has always been more than a season to me. It is a reminder of the cold days when hope was the only thing that kept me warm. As snow covered the streets in white, I imagined it washing away fear and making room for new beginnings. Every snowflake reminded me that even in the harshest seasons, something beautiful can survive.
 
I made a promise to myself that winter: no matter how difficult life became, I would never stop chasing my dreams. 

My story began long before I understood what dreams truly meant. At the age of six, while many children spent their days playing, I learned to weave carpets. My small hands carefully tied thousands of knots, one after another. Every thread carried not only the weight of hard work but also the hope that one day I could continue my education, support my family, and build a different future. 

As the years passed, life became even harder. I worked both inside and outside my home. There were days when exhaustion made me feel as if I could not take another step. Yet every morning I reminded myself that giving up would never change my life. If doors did not open for me, I would build my own. 

Carpet weaving was never just a job. It became the language of my dreams. Every knot I tied whispered the same message: Keep going. Don't stop. 

Life is never a straight road. Sometimes it lifts you to the highest mountain, and sometimes it leaves you in the deepest valley. I experienced both. There were moments of joy, but there were also moments when I questioned whether all my efforts were worth it. Still, I learned that every season passes, and every hardship carries a lesson. 

School became the turning point of my life. It opened my eyes to a world beyond poverty and struggle. It taught me that education is not simply about books; it is about discovering my own strength. Most importantly, it showed me that no one succeeds completely alone. Sometimes, all it takes is one person who believes in you. 

I will never forget March 21, 2021. 

It was the first time I had ever failed an exam. 

I felt as though the world had collapsed around me. I kept asking myself, How can I face my family? They had sacrificed so much for my education, and I believed I had disappointed them. The pain became even greater when some of my classmates laughed at me. Their laughter echoed in my mind, making me feel small, ashamed, and completely alone. 

Then my teacher quietly walked toward me. 
She looked into my eyes and said,"This failure is not your ending. It can become your new beginning. The choice is yours. I believe in you. One day, you will surprise yourself with what you achieve. Ignore the voices that try to break you, and let this failure become the greatest lesson of your life." 

Those words changed everything. 

For the first time, I realized that failure is not the opposite of success—it is often the first step toward it. My teacher gave me something far more valuable than encouragement. She gave me belief in myself when I had lost it completely.

Today, I still carry the memories of every hardship. I remember being forced to leave my classroom because I could not afford the fees. I remember standing in front of my classmates while they laughed at my poverty. I remember returning home with tears in my eyes, wondering if my dreams were simply too expensive for someone like me. 

But I also remember standing back up. 

I have been weaving carpets since I was six years old. Today, at seventeen, I have woven far more than carpets. I have woven resilience, courage, patience, and hope into my life. Every challenge became another thread that made me stronger instead of weaker.
 
My dream is no longer only to change my own life. 

I dream of becoming a successful business leader who creates opportunities for others, especially girls who have been told that their dreams are impossible. I want to build businesses that provide jobs, support families, and remind young people that their circumstances do not define their future. 

The threads of the carpets I weave may one day wear out with time. 

But the dreams woven into my heart never will. 

As long as I continue believing in myself, no hardship will ever be stronger than the future I am determined to create. 

This is my story, but it is also the story of many girls whose dreams are tested by poverty, hardship, and inequality. I hope my journey reminds them that resilience can transform pain into purpose, and that every small step forward brings us closer to a brighter future. Dreams may begin as fragile threads, but with courage, faith, and perseverance, they can be woven into a life filled with hope.

stories.title: The Ending That Became My Beginning
stories.description: After the loss of her education and livelihood, Maryam transforms grief into purpose by founding an educational center for orphaned and working children in Bamyan. This inspiring personal narrative explores resilience, the healing power of education, and how hope can emerge even after life's most painful endings.
stories.authorBio:
Maryam Halimi is a young woman from Afghanistan, active as a social entrepreneur, educator, and community development professional, with over 8 years of experience designing and implementing initiatives in education, youth leadership, and women’s empowerment. She founded KUDAC NGO in 2022 to expand educational opportunities for children from struggling backgrounds. Over the past 5 years, KUDAC has served more than 220 children. Maryam has also trained over 220 women and led a volunteer team in delivering sustainable, community-driven programs. She says, “I value education, and seeing young children working on the streets prompted me to create a way to let education improve their lives. Of course, education is more than being able to read, but a core component of a promising future.” 
Today, she continues to work to empower communities and individuals with the knowledge, skills, and opportunities they need to find their own paths and build successful futures.
stories.content:
Everywhere smelled of dust and a painfully heavy quiet. The tables and chairs that once witnessed endless laughter, conversations, and the youth's dreams were now buried deep beneath layers of dust. Each corner of the restaurant brought back memories of days I had built with love and lived with hope. As I closed the doors for the last time, it was as if I had lost a part of my identity. The farewell tasted bitter, like burnt coffee lingering on my soul.  

Farewell, Princess-Maryam Restaurant.  

The city was the same, yet it was nothing like before. The women and girls in bright clothing and makeup had disappeared from the streets of the city, and I was no longer called “Princess”. As my books and notebooks were gathering dust in the corner, I had no idea when I would be able to sit in a classroom again. My academic dreams, like many other dreams of mine, felt distant and unobtainable.  

I spent days suffocated with confusion, having no clue where to restart or how to accept the way my life had changed overnight. 
 
But I am not someone to give up.  

The real battle was inside me. Every single day, I had to choose between hope and hopelessness. Slowly putting my broken pieces back together, I rebuilt a new, stronger me. This time, I forged a new path over the broken one. One that would lead to knowledge, a basic right that was taken away from women and girls of my nation.  

In those days, KUDAC Educational Center was born, a safe space for growth, for many kids who needed hope more than anything else, and myself. It was built in Bamyan for orphans and working children. At first, I believed I was the one creating a safe hideaway for the kids, yet it turned out these kids became the real safe hideaway for my tired soul. Many of these kids had never experienced the real warmth of parents and a family. The small hands that were meant to be holding a pen and paper instead bore scars of labor. Despite everything, the flame of hope in their eyes was the warmth my soul needed.  

It’s unfair to call KUDAC just an educational center. Although the kids learn how to read and write here, that is not the whole story. They also learn how to express themselves as confident individuals. They learn that being kind is not a weakness but a strength. The kids who did not have time to dream because they had to work learned to dream fearlessly. Each time I see a huge smile that shows a fallen tooth or a dream that is painted with childish innocence, they remind me that education can change lives. 
 
As the laughter of children echoes in the halls of KUDAC, a warmth spreads through my chest. They remind me that closing some doors does not mean the end; instead, they could be the beginning of something new, something more beautiful. And each time, without fail, it makes me smile. It is my motivation for trying to work hard so that I can help build a safer, brighter, and happier future for them. What I once thought was failure and my downfall turned out to be a path guiding me toward something far greater, something that helped me find the purpose of my life.

stories.title: Broken Dream
stories.description: This heartfelt personal narrative follows Tamana's journey from being the top student in her class to earning a place in medical school, only to have her education cut short by the Taliban's return to power. Despite overwhelming setbacks, her story is one of resilience, hope, and an unwavering determination to one day wear her white coat again.
stories.imageCredit: Image taken from https://pin.it/7pUoTlbkD, by the author
stories.authorBio: Tamanna Sadaat is a girl from Afghanistan, where her education was interrupted after universities were closed to women. Despite these challenges, she continues to study through online courses and seeks opportunities to continue her education. She hopes to one day return to medical school, become a doctor, and use her story to give voice to the resilience, hope, and determination of girls whose dreams have been put on hold.
stories.content:
I come from a humble family, but I have always been full of hopes and dreams. I started school with great expectations. From my very first day, I made a promise to myself: I would never surrender to the difficulties of life. I would remain strong and determined so that I could achieve my goals. 

I knew that I had to work hard. From the first grade, I studied with passion and enthusiasm. I loved my education and my dreams in the way that a mother cares for and nurtures her child. Every day that passed, I felt that I was getting closer to the future I had imagined for myself.
 
From first grade until twelfth grade, I was always the top student in my class. When I graduated from high school, I finished as the top student overall. Despite the financial difficulties my family faced, I began preparing for the university entrance exam with determination. I did not want to become a burden on my family. Instead, I taught students at home and used the small income I earned to pay for my own education. 

I never gave up. Through the cold winters and hot summers, I continued my studies. My mind was focused on one goal: succeeding in the entrance exam and being admitted to the field I loved. I wanted to fulfill my father’s dream and make my family proud. 

I worked tirelessly, day and night. The day before the entrance exam, tears filled my eyes because I remembered all the hardships I had endured to reach that moment. I took the exam with great hope and waited anxiously for the results. 

When the results were announced, I was overwhelmed with stress. I wondered whether all my sacrifices and efforts would finally pay off. Then, by the grace of God and the reward of my hard work, I achieved my dream. I was accepted into the Faculty of Medicine with high marks. 

My family and I cried tears of joy. I was happier than I had ever been in my life. On my first day at university, I felt like the luckiest person in the world. The first time I wore my white medical coat, I felt as if I had entered a new world filled with happiness and hope. 

But that happiness did not last long.
When the Taliban returned to power, my dreams and the dreams of countless other girls were buried beneath the dust. I fell into deep depression. For two years, I felt like a silent and lifeless person. Nothing seemed to help. No medicine and no effort could ease the pain I carried inside. 

After two years, I realized that life was still moving forward and that I had to stand on my own feet again. I began taking online courses and worked hard to find scholarship opportunities. However, because of financial difficulties, I was unable to pursue many of them. Some scholarships that seemed suitable had age restrictions or language requirements that I could not meet. These obstacles caused me even more pain. 

Sometimes I ask myself: Is this fair? I have the talent and the determination, but I do not have the opportunity. Will there ever be a day when I can return to university? Will there ever be someone in this world who will help girls like me, girls whose hearts are filled with dreams but whose paths to education have been blocked? 

I still believe in education. I still believe in hope. And despite everything that has happened, I continue to dream of the day when I can return to my studies, wear my white coat again, and serve humanity as a doctor. 

My dream has been delayed, but it has not been destroyed.

stories.title: The Pages That Shaped Me: A Journey Through Books and Becoming
stories.description: In this reflective essay, Maria explores how books became a source of hope, resilience, and self-discovery when access to formal education was limited. Through the lessons found in literature, she discovers the power of knowledge to shape identity, overcome adversity, and inspire a future defined not by circumstance, but by purpose.
stories.imageCredit: Image taken from https://pin.it/3fUsxToSI, by the author
stories.authorBio: Maria Alokozay is a Health Science student at the University of the People (UoPeople). She is passionate about education, public health, and storytelling as a tool for empowerment. Her experiences as an Afghan student navigating challenges in education have shaped her belief in resilience, lifelong learning, and the transformative power of knowledge. Through her writing, she hopes to amplify the voices of girls who continue to pursue education despite barriers and to contribute to a future where access to learning is a universal right.
stories.content:
Perhaps no encounter in life is truly accidental—not even my encounter with the books that held my hand during lonely days and guided me through walls of silence toward brighter horizons of understanding. In those moments, books were more than a source of entertainment; they became a refuge, a doorway out of a world that sometimes felt smaller than my dreams. When the doors of formal education were closed to me, books became my unconventional classrooms, and every chapter I turned was a step away from the shadows of doubt and into the light of self-discovery. 

When I first read There Are No Coincidences, I did not realize that each page had the power to slowly reshape my way of thinking. It taught me to look for patterns in the chaos of my daily life, finding meaning even in the most restricted environments. Later, the Alchemist taught me that the greatest treasures are not always found in distant places; sometimes, they lie within ourselves. In Santiago's journey, I saw reflections of my own path—a journey where deserts are not always geographical landscapes, but can also be silence, limitations, and loneliness. That book forced me to confront the fear of the unknown and embrace my own personal legend, even when the road seemed impassable. 

Along the way, other books taught me that growth is the result of small but consistent efforts. From The Compound Effect, I learned that meaningful change begins with simple daily choices. I realized that my situation, however difficult, could not stop the momentum of my own intellectual expansion if I remained consistent. From Viktor Frankl, I learned that even in the most difficult circumstances, human beings can find a reason to keep going. His words became my anchor, reminding me that while I could not choose my circumstances, I could always choose my attitude toward them. These ideas were never just theories to me; they became tools for resilience that helped me navigate the psychological toll of being a student in a system that often denied my right to learn. 

During times when the world around me felt quieter than ever, the pages of books gave me a voice to listen to. Through reading The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People, I came to understand that life is not a finished project but an ongoing process of conscious choices. I learned that the responsibility for building my life rests on my own shoulders, even when circumstances are far from ideal. Books taught me that people can rise above limitations; that discipline is not merely a habit, but a quiet form of resistance against the chaos of life. Every small step and every daily effort contributes to the creation of a greater future. When I study Health Science today, I am guided by this same discipline, understanding that my ambition to contribute to public health is a direct result of these early lessons in self-management. 

Perhaps the most important lesson books have taught me can be summarized in this thought: everything unfolds in its own time. The difference between people is that some wait for life to come to them, while others rise and create their own paths. I have learned that there are no shortcuts to growth. A mature person is someone who embraces life with all its ups and downs, contradictions, and uncertainties—someone who understands that patience does not mean standing still, but moving forward consciously through hardship. This patience has been my strongest ally, allowing me to persist in my studies and my advocacy despite the many obstacles placed in my way. 

Books have shown me that identity is not fixed; it is shaped by the choices we make every day. Every idea that found its way into my mind brought me one step closer to understanding myself. I learned that true power lies in awareness, not in circumstances. I have realized that my struggle is not unique, but my response to it can be. By reading widely, I have connected with the wisdom of centuries, realizing that others have stood in my shoes and found ways to thrive. This realization has been deeply empowering. 

Today, when I reflect on my journey, I realize that books have helped shape the direction of my life. They have taught me that knowledge is not only for learning but also for building meaning, purpose, and a future that may once have seemed out of reach. I have transitioned from being a girl who feared the silence to a student who uses her voice to contribute to a better understanding of public health and education. The knowledge I acquire is not just information; it is the building block for the reality I hope to see in my country. 

I read these books to understand that every person has the ability to rewrite their own story. And with that belief, I know that even in the midst of limitations, it is still possible to write, to create, and to move forward. Every word I put on paper reminds me of this truth: real growth begins within us, not in the conditions that surround us. My journey is far from over, but I now walk it with the certainty that my mind is free, my purpose is defined, and my story is one that I am actively writing every single day. I hope that by sharing this, I can encourage other girls to find their own refuge in the power of words and to continue their journey of becoming, no matter how difficult the road may seem.

stories.title: A Mind That Refused to Be Closed
stories.description: From growing up as an Afghan refugee in Iran to pursuing higher education against extraordinary odds, this personal narrative is a testament to resilience, perseverance, and an unwavering love of learning. It reflects on the barriers faced by refugee students while affirming that, even when opportunities are taken away, hope and determination can endure.
stories.authorBio: Narges is an Afghan educator, translator, and aspiring scientist currently living in Afghanistan. Born and raised in Iran as a refugee, she studied  Cellular and Molecular Biology at university and worked as a laboratory technician in a public hospital in Iran. She has been teaching English since  2022 and also works as an English translator. Narges achieved an IELTS  score of 7 and continues to pursue her passion for languages by studying  Chinese and German (A1–A2 levels). She is also a practitioner of Hapkido martial arts. Deeply passionate about education, science, music, and language learning, she believes that learning is a lifelong journey. In her free time, she enjoys reading books and exploring new ideas.
stories.content:
Some dreams begin quietly—in small rooms, in families who have almost nothing except hope. I was born in Iran as a refugee into a kind and supportive Afghan family. To my parents, education meant everything. From the time I was very young, they emphasized the importance of learning and encouraged me to explore the world through books. I loved reading, writing,  and discovering new things. With my mother's support and my passion for learning, I was able to read and write simple Persian sentences by the age of four, and books quickly became my favorite companions. 

Life as a refugee in Iran was never easy. Every year, my family had to pay a large amount of money simply to be allowed to remain there. Despite these hardships, my father enrolled me in English classes when I was in third grade. I was the youngest student in the class; most of the others were over fifteen years old. Because I began learning English at such a young age, I was able to complete the program by the age of sixteen and achieve an IELTS  qualification. English soon became one of my strongest subjects.

To make a long story short, with the continuous support of my parents, I  graduated from high school as the top student in the natural sciences stream,  despite the discrimination that Afghan students often faced. Then came the most important moment of my academic life: the university entrance examination. I devoted nearly all my time to preparing for it. I sacrificed leisure, rest, and many simple joys because I believed that education was the key to a better future. 

When the day of the exam arrived, I felt both nervous and hopeful. However,  when I received the exam paper, I noticed something painful on the first page: a space for the national identification number. Afghan refugees in Iran do not have Iranian national ID cards, which meant we had to leave that section blank. In that moment, it felt like a silent reminder that I was not considered equal to the others. It was a painful indication that the system had not been designed for someone like me. 

As you might expect, I was unable to qualify for medicine at a public university, where tuition was free. Still, my parents refused to let me give up on my dreams. They encouraged me to enroll in a private university instead.  Although the tuition fees were expensive for my family, my father worked tirelessly to support my education. 

I began studying Cellular and Molecular Biology. I studied with determination and dedication, and soon I became the top student in my class among both male and female students. I was also the only Afghan student in the program. My professors often praised my hard work and commitment.  Those were the moments when I truly felt the strength of being a girl. Every time I raised my hand to answer a question and every time my professors recognized my efforts, I felt empowered. I felt that all the struggles of my parents and all the sacrifices we had made were not in vain. 

I dreamed of continuing my education until I earned a PhD. However, after two years at university, a new regulation was introduced for Afghan students:  they were required to have a passport in order to continue their studies. At that time, I only had a legal residence card. We tried to obtain a passport through the Afghan embassy in Iran, but unfortunately, it was 2023, shortly after the Taliban returned to power in Afghanistan, and the process became extremely slow. 

Because time was passing and I could not risk losing my education, my family decided to travel to Afghanistan to obtain my passport more quickly and then return to Iran so that I could continue my studies. But life does not always follow our plans. After we arrived in Afghanistan and obtained my passport, we were unable to return to Iran because of the political situation and regional instability. 

My university education came to a sudden and painful end. Today, I am in  Afghanistan, and I cannot continue my university studies. Sometimes this reality makes me feel deeply sad, but my love for learning has never disappeared. Currently, I am studying the Chinese language and continuing to educate myself in every way possible. Education is not simply something I  want; it is part of who I am. 

I still believe that one day universities will reopen their doors to girls. And even if every door remains closed, I will build my own path and continue my education. Because I have learned something important from my life:  strength is not only about achieving your dreams; it is about refusing to abandon them, even when the world tries to stop you. I will not be satisfied with only two years of university education. One day, I will achieve my dream and earn my PhD. When that day comes, I will make my parents proud, honor the sacrifices they made for me, and once again feel the true strength of being a girl.

stories.title: The Bitter Silence of Our Alley
stories.description: Set against the backdrop of Kabul's fall in August 2021, this personal narrative follows a young girl through her final day at school before everything changed. Blending memory with the quiet symbolism of a snow-covered alley, the story reflects on loss, resilience, and the enduring hope that even the smallest act can leave a lasting mark.
stories.authorBio:
Mitra Komak was born and raised in Kabul, Afghanistan. She finished her primary and secondary school education in Kabul and her postsecondary studies via online learning since 2021. 
She joined academic programs such as TTS at AUAF. She is currently a Computer Science Student at AUAF, continuing her studies online.
Additionally, she is attending the HTML & CSS Workshop in the Empower Her Initiative to improve her skills.
stories.content:
The sky was just beginning to brighten, but our alley was unusually empty. The bare branches of the trees stretching over the yards were covered with glistening white snow that shimmered softly for anyone who walked by. The air in Kabul was cold, smoky, and filled with the stillness of winter, but it felt as though another kind of cold had settled over the city first—a cold that could not melt with the changing seasons.

Though it was no longer early morning, there was no sign of girls and boys leaving for school. Their footprints were nowhere to be found in the fresh snow that had fallen during the night. The alley was eerily quiet. There was no laughter echoing through the streets, no children playing in the snow, no movement that usually brought the neighborhood to life. Even the women passing by walked quickly with their heads lowered, as if carrying burdens too heavy to speak aloud.

It was a familiar yet sinister silence. It was as though I had felt it before, many years ago. My heart tightened, and tears filled my eyes like a curtain slowly falling. My thoughts carried me back—five years and a few months—to the day I went to school for the last time.

That day, I had a history and geography exam. The night before, I stayed up late surrounded by books and notes, trying to review everything one last time. At 5:30 in the morning, I woke up, put on my beautiful blue-and-white school uniform, wrapped a white scarf around my head, and carried my books to the kitchen, where my mother had already prepared breakfast. I hurried out the door, boarded the bus, and spent the ride reviewing the most difficult parts of my lessons.

Although I was completely focused on my books that morning, everything around me felt different. There was an unusual silence, something unsettling in the air. Still, I ignored it. I was just a student, concerned only with passing my exams.

When I arrived at school, I looked for my friend in the courtyard. Students sat quietly with their books, some anxiously reviewing their notes while others studied with determined focus. There was only one thought in my mind: "How am I going to pass these exams?"

After the exam, I waited nearly an hour to speak with one of my teachers. I was exhausted. My friend and I bought some juice and cake, sat together in one of the classrooms, and talked for a while.

By then, news had already begun spreading that province after province was falling. Yet I never imagined Kabul would fall. I simply could not believe that something so enormous could happen without a long and devastating war.

As my friend and I continued talking, a man I had never seen before entered the classroom. In a loud voice, he told everyone to leave the school and go home immediately. I assumed he worked with the school's security team. He quickly moved from one classroom to another, repeating the same urgent message.

I threw my unfinished juice and cake into the trash and reached for my friend's hand. Confused, she asked, "What is going on?"

I looked at her and said quietly, "Perhaps Kabul has fallen. Let's go home."

A strange uneasiness spread through my body. Holding hands, we ran down the long school corridors. I remember feeling grateful that she was beside me.

Instead of taking the main road outside the school gate, we chose a smaller side street and ran faster and faster.

Police vehicles sped past us with their sirens blaring. Everywhere there was confusion. Some people stood frozen in shock while others rushed to close their shops.

Suddenly, a woman stopped me and asked, "What is happening? Did the Taliban take over?"

I couldn't answer. I simply shook my head and kept running.

Eventually, after what felt like hours, I reached our alley.

It was empty.

Too empty.

My steps slowed. The silence pressed down on me like a weight, as though darkness itself had settled over the neighborhood. I walked carefully toward our house, afraid of what I might find.

When I reached the gate, my brother was standing outside. My mother waited anxiously in the yard.

The moment I saw them, I ran into my mother's arms.

For the first time, I cried in front of her without holding anything back. I clung to her as though she were the only safe place left in the world.

The day after that, nothing was ever the same.

Although the sky remained blue, it no longer seemed beautiful. The birds no longer sounded joyful. A sadness settled over every street and every home.

The alley became more crowded, yet somehow darker and quieter than ever before. There were no girls playing outside. No cheerful voices drifted through the neighborhood. Only silent windows stared into the distance, waiting for something that would never return.

Even now, I can still remember the feeling of those two schoolbooks in my hands on that exam day, as though time itself had stopped.

I checked the time. I was already late.

Carrying fresh bread, I hurried back home through the snowy alley. As I walked, I noticed something that made me stop for just a moment.

My footprints were the first footprints of a girl on the untouched snow, breaking the silence.

It felt as though, even in a country where there was hardly any room left for girls, a small trace of freedom still remained.

stories.title: Hungry Minds Need Food
stories.description: A moving reflection on four years without education, this poem captures the quiet grief, resilience, and fading hope of Afghan girls whose dreams have been suspended by oppression. Through powerful imagery, it explores what it means to lose not only classrooms, but time, opportunity, and the words to imagine a different future.
stories.authorBio: Nadia Sakhi is an Afghan poet and writer whose work explores silence, absence, grief, and forgotten dreams. She writes to preserve what time tries to erase.
stories.content:
Today, we celebrate the fourth year of deprivation,

The candle is waiting for us,
to blow it out,

We blow out the candle,
knowing that after its extinction,
only darkness remains,

And that is exactly what they want. 

We must walk on a dark road,

As if silence has swallowed darkness,
and darkness has swallowed silence,

Today marks 1,460 days
that we have been imprisoned within walls,

Perhaps I counted wrong,
more or less,

We have lost track of numbers,

The pen is broken,

Its ink stands farther away than itself,

The pencils have been sharpened to their very end,

The doors of drawing
are not open to us,

I saw the flames
of burned notebooks
in a corner,

The colors have dried,

The roots of knowledge are thirsty,
they need water,

Our minds are hungry,
they need food,

Our minds lie asleep in darkness,
Not one,
not two,
But millions of silenced thoughts,

Our ideas have been cut short,
trimmed away,

The story is long,
But the ink is little,

I fear half the story
will remain for next year,

I fear the ink will run out,

But the words will remain,

Days pass like hours,

years pass like days,

Our fear is not of existence,

We fear that time
will not stand by us,

We fear reaching the final period
without having read,

We fear not living
for the tomorrow
we dreamed into being,

We fear our notebooks
will remain empty forever,

We fear that one day
we will no longer be able to write,

We fear forgetting words,

We fear the day
when the pages of bookswill no longer remember us,

We are simply afraid!

Our dreams are in flight,
Suspended between sky and earth,
Like clouds,
They cannot stay with us,
Nor can they find peace in the sky,

Our lips hum a melody,
Meaningless,
A melody whose meaning
we do not know,
We look at the sky,
The earth,
And ourselves,
Nothing!

Like sand,
we are escaping through cracks,
Even if only a little,
"A little place to live,
and a little place to die."

Under the heat of the sun,
we searched for what was lost,

That lost thing
without which
we cannot find the bright path,

We are wandering,

We did not succeed,
It is not here!

Perhaps one day it will come,

But what a pity,
By then,
we will be bigger,

And it
will be smaller.

stories.title: The Forbidden Door Did Not Break Me
stories.description: The Forbidden Door Did Not Break Me is a powerful personal narrative about the day Afghan women were barred from returning to university under Taliban rule. Through Nilab's journey to take an anatomy exam, the story explores the loss of education, the courage to speak in the face of oppression, and the quiet resilience that continues to unite Afghan girls despite extraordinary barriers.
stories.authorBio: Nilab Mohammadi is passionate about storytelling and self-expression. Once aspiring to become a doctor, she found a different way to connect with others through the written word. Her work reflects on resilience, identity, and the strength found in navigating life's unexpected turns.
stories.content:
Fall nights are long, but when grief sits in your throat like a stone, they turn into eternity. The announcement banning education for women replayed endlessly in my mind, making me turn my pillow over and over and preventing me from closing my eyes.

At 7:00 a.m., I finally rose from bed. The sky was covered with dark clouds, as if it too were grieving, shedding its tears through a light drizzle.

I dressed and gathered my books as usual. I had an anatomy exam to take.
An hour later, I reached the university gate. My heart beat so loudly that I felt everyone could hear it. The street was filled with honking cars and shouting fruit vendors, but the university sidewalk felt haunted, as if time itself had frozen.

A crowd of other girls stood near the entrance, books in hand, their faces exhausted as though their eyelids were too heavy for their eyes. Like me, they had studied. Like me, they dreamed of becoming doctors.
My eyes settled on a girl holding the same anatomy book as mine.
We stood barely one meter from the gate, waiting to enter our class and take our exam.

Yet the place that had once felt like a dream was now illegal for me to enter. The threshold I had always crossed with pride now lay forbidden beneath my feet.

I noticed a newly painted sentence in red:
"Women are not allowed to enter."

It was the same sentence I had seen on television the night before.
"The Taliban soldiers are coming to control you girls. Please leave, or you will get me in trouble," said Kaka Qurban, our school's janitor.
"We'll wait quietly. They will have mercy and allow us in," cried one girl.

"Let's ask them nicely," another replied.

My own lips parted, then closed again.

I had taken one step closer when a deafening shout shattered the silence. Three armed men in black attire stormed toward us, rifles slung across their chests.

"STOP! STOP, hamshira (sisters)! Why are you here?"
The tallest one turned to Kaka Qurban.

"Why didn't you tell them they cannot come to school?"
The janitor lowered his eyes obediently.

"They say they want to take their exam."

Heat rushed into the soldier's face.

"What the hell are they doing here without a mahram (male companion)?"

Then he turned to us.
"Where is your nobility? Your haya, your sharm? What kind of fathers and brothers allow this?"

A silence settled over us.

Should we be ashamed for simply wanting to learn?

No, my mind screamed.

But my lips remained still.

"Only dishonorable fathers allow a girl to be in a class with boys," the soldier said, displaying a sharp, sarcastic smile beside his rifle. "Your time of immodesty is done."

Something inside me shattered.

Perhaps it was the nights I had studied until dawn, my eyes burning from exhaustion. Or my mother's tired, wrinkled face, leaving before sunrise each day and returning home with enough money to buy me a notebook.

Whatever it was, it overcame my fear.

"What should we be ashamed of?" I asked.

My trembling voice barely pushed the words into the world.

Still, it was enough.

My spine straightened.

In that moment, I became more than myself.

I became every Afghan girl told to stay home, told that she deserved only black fabric and silence.

I was my mother, who had once been banished from university.

I was every woman who had never been asked whether she agreed to her own marriage.

I was the entire crowd labeled dishonorable simply for wanting to take an exam.

The soldier glared at me, but his gaze did not weaken me. It made me speak louder.

"What should we be ashamed of?" I repeated. "For curing your mother? Your sisters? Or your wife during childbirth?"

A silence stronger than any bomb surrounded us.

I pressed my anatomy book tightly against my chest, afraid someone might snatch it away.

I knew about the veins and arteries of the human heart, but in that moment I learned something deeper about my own.

I learned that I did not need to carry a gun or possess great physical strength to be considered strong.

I could be strong in my fragile womanhood.

"Shut up! Be haya!" the enforcer roared.

He stepped toward us, rifle raised, boots slamming into the wet ground.
The girls around me grabbed my sleeves, trying to pull me behind them. My heart pounded so fiercely—with fear and with the strength of our shared cause—that I barely heard what they were saying.

I knew I should retreat.

Kaka Qurban was pleading.

"Please, please, Taliban Sahib. They are just teenage girls. They are heartbroken and do not know how to behave."

The soldier snatched my anatomy book and threw it into the mud.

"You think you are going to save my family's life someday? Who will save you this moment from my hand?"

Time froze.

The mud beneath my feet felt heavier, as though it wanted to pull me under.
"Leave!" he roared, pointing his gun.

The girls stepped back.

But I remained where I was, staring directly at him.

Cold blood seemed to course through my body, yet some invisible force held me upright.

I bent down, picked up my book from the mud, and began wiping it clean with my scarf.

A nearby girl knelt beside me and helped with her own scarf.

I nodded in gratitude, too overwhelmed to speak.

Then I pressed the book against my chest and walked away.

I did not take my anatomy exam.

Yet that day awakened something inside me.

As I walked away, still shaking, I caught sight of several girls watching me.

Hidden smiles of encouragement spread across their faces.

I walked taller, knowing that I was not alone.

stories.title: Finding My Direction
stories.description: This reflection describes how EmpowerHer’s Resume Building Workshop transformed the author’s understanding of her own experiences and achievements. Alongside lessons from The Alchemist and The Little Prince, the workshop helped her gain confidence, recognize her growth, and move forward with purpose as a medical student.
stories.imageAlt: An untitled painting by Mursal Ahmadzai
stories.authorBio: Zahra Darmani is a medical student at Al-Farabi Kazakh National University, an avid reader, and a passionate advocate for education, personal growth, and community empowerment.
stories.content:
When I participated in EmpowerHer's Resume Building Workshop, it unexpectedly became more than just a class. I learned to view my own experiences in a completely different light. I had always considered a resume as just a simple sheet of paper listing skills and experiences. However, as the workshop progressed, it revealed itself to be something much more significant. To me, it became a way of reflecting on how much I have learned and accomplished, and of giving myself the recognition I deserve.

I learned to express my strengths in words, confidently discuss my development, and frame my experiences as a coherent narrative of personal growth. What started as a technical tutorial surprisingly turned into an inner revelation. The workshop showed me that I do have achievements worth sharing, aspirations worth pursuing, and doors that are truly opening. It taught me to trust my abilities, stay organized, and move toward the future with intention and courage.

Of course, the workshop benefited my practical development; in addition, a couple of books have been emotional and reflective guides throughout my life. The Alchemist and The Little Prince are two that have stayed with me for a long time, and I want to share some of the lessons they’ve taught me.

The Alchemist taught me something unexpected: that following a dream is worthwhile, even when you can’t see where it leads. Santiago’s journey felt familiar. The doubts he faced, the fear of failure, the moments when giving up seemed easier—I’ve been there too. But what really stuck with me was the idea: “When we strive to become better, everything around us becomes better too.” It helped me understand that focusing on my own development is both necessary and valuable. It truly changes things around you. When I sat down to build my resume during the workshop, I kept thinking about that. I didn’t want to play small or hide what I really wanted. I wanted to be honest about my ambitions, even if they felt big.

The Little Prince, in its simple and beautiful way, taught me to look deeper. Instead of focusing only on results or achievements, it reminded me that meaning often comes from care, intention, and connection. The book encouraged me to value the lessons hidden in ordinary experiences, and to see that my journey matters even when it feels quiet or slow. This helped me appreciate the small steps in my life that I used to overlook.

These books have kept me grounded and motivated, while the Resume Building Workshop helped me put my goals into words. Now, as I continue my studies at Al-Farabi Kazakh National University as a medical student, I carry with me what I learned from both the books and EmpowerHer: the courage to move forward, the intention to shape my own story, and the belief that every step matters.

stories.title: Fire Riders of the Mountains
stories.description: A poetic story about a mountain woman whose calm, stone-like strength hides an inner fire of learning, resilience, and hope. Through knowledge, connection, and shared courage, her inner flame grows and spreads to other women, creating quiet but powerful change.
stories.authorBio: Suhaila Naweed is a young Afghan artist, educator, and technology enthusiast passionate about learning and storytelling. Through EmpowerHer, she continued her education online, developed new skills, and found inspiration to grow. Her work highlights the strength and hope of Afghan women and the power of creativity to create change.
stories.content:
High in the mountains, where silence lives between the rocks and the wind carries stories through the valleys, a woman stood.

Her face looked like stone—strong, calm, and shaped by time. But through the cracks in that stone, fire was glowing. It was not a fire that burned or destroyed. It was a fire that gave warmth, light, and life.

The stone on her face carried the weight of many hard days, cold winters, long struggles, and quiet endurance. It reflected the life of a land where people learn to survive storms, losses, and silence. Yet inside that stone lived a flame—a symbol of strength and hope. A fire that belonged not only to her but to many women like her.

At night, when the mountains became quiet and the world slowed down, she looked at the glowing screen in front of her. There, paths of learning and connection opened. Through simple lessons, shared knowledge, and inspiring conversations, new doors appeared. Small opportunities created big changes. Each new skill, each new idea became another spark in her fire.

But her fire was not only for herself. She shared it—in her words, actions, and courage.

Every step the women took became a spark for other women. Every choice became a light for someone else. Together, they became the Fire Riders of the mountains—women who carry light through hard places, who bring warmth into cold lives, who turn silence into voice.

When cold winds touched her face, she understood something deeply—that true fire lives inside. It cannot be stolen, it cannot be destroyed or silenced.

This fire was built from learning, service, creativity, and shared strength. It grew through connection, guidance, and through spaces that gave women the chance to grow and believe in themselves again.

Life was not easy. Limits existed. Pressure existed. Fear existed.

But the fire stayed.

She learned that stone may look strong and cold, but inside it, hidden energy always moves. And inside women, hidden power always lives.

Sometimes she remembered old mountain stories—stories of brave women, quiet heroes, and unseen strength. But this was not only a story from the past.

This fire was real; it lived now in real women, real lives, struggles, and dreams.

When the sun rose behind the peaks, the fire still glowed. Not loud. Not violent. Not wild. But steady, alive, unstoppable.

She stood as a symbol, not just of one woman, but of many. A symbol of learning, resilience, quiet power, and shared light.

And in the meeting of stone and fire, the message remained:

Real strength is not what the world sees.  
Real power is what the heart carries.  
And real change begins when one flame becomes many.

And somewhere between stone and flame, a new future begins…

For Afghan women, the quit keepers of fire.

24/1/2026

stories.title: I Hope I Don't Forget Myself
stories.description: This story reflects on a girl’s lost childhood freedom and the sudden silence that followed when her education and public life were taken away. Through painting, she transforms grief, anger, and injustice into art, using creativity as a powerful form of resistance and self‑expression.
stories.authorBio: I am an Afghan student, former English teacher, and community leader who continues to empower girls and reflect their experiences through education, art, and writing despite restrictions.
stories.content:
I remember the schoolyard in summer.
The ground was warm beneath our feet, and the air carried our laughter far beyond the walls. Our hair was loose, tangled in the wind, and our hearts were lighter than we knew. We played volleyball without thinking about time, without fear, without understanding how temporary those moments were. Back then, freedom didn’t need a definition. It was simply life.

Sometimes I ask myself if that girl was really me.  
The girl who laughed easily.  
The girl who ran without hesitation.  
The girl who believed tomorrow would always arrive gently.

I am not sure when everything changed. I only know that one day, it did.

School disappeared—not slowly, not gradually, but all at once. The gate closed. The voices faded. The schoolyard fell silent. Friends became memories instead of classmates. The volleyball stayed untouched, and without realizing it, I forgot how to play. It sounds small, but it isn’t. When a girl forgets how to play, it means something much bigger has been taken from her.

My world grew smaller.  
My days grew quieter.  
Too quiet.

I was told this was for my safety.  
I was told this was religion.  
I was told this was how life should be now.  
But nothing about it felt just.

I couldn’t raise my voice, so I found another way to speak.  
I started to paint.

At first, I didn’t plan what would appear on the page. My hands moved faster than my thoughts. Faces emerged—distorted, angry, empty. Guns. Shadows. Fear pressed into color. I painted women trapped inside rules, walls, and violence. I painted what I saw around me and what I carried inside me: grief, rage, and questions no one wanted to answer.

In one painting, a man stands armed, surrounded by darkness. In front of him, a woman is reduced to silence—even in death. I didn’t paint this to shock. I painted it because this is what power looks like when it has no conscience. Because some truths are too heavy for words, and only art can hold them.

Painting became my resistance.

When I paint, I am not obedient.  
I am not invisible.  
I am not silent.  
I am honest.

Art gave me a place where no one could interrupt me or tell me that my feelings were wrong. Every brushstroke became proof that I still existed—that my mind was still free, even when my body was confined.

![Paintings done by Mahboba Mushtaq](https://3625xubr2k.ufs.sh/f/yiXnwfSQWCPTK0t4vXCVy1oGkRMuS0Lravl9JbQIxWFcNhtq)
![Paintings done by Mahboba Mushtaq](https://3625xubr2k.ufs.sh/f/yiXnwfSQWCPTjTT24XzsfkIRBuYnTVcl8O9LdXP5103pNyJU)

stories.title: Silent Girls
stories.description: A poignant poem portraying the daily life of girls denied education and freedom, showing their silent suffering, endurance, and the small but unbreakable hope they carry within.
stories.authorBio: This is Maroofa Mohammadi, someone who loves writing, learning, and working to improve her skills, find her voice, and build strong confidence through writing.
stories.content:
> Morning rises,
>
> but not for play,
>
> not for school,
>
> only for chores that steal the day.



> They wake with the sun,
>
> bags empty,
>
> hearts heavy,
>
> dreams locked behind doors they cannot open.



> The walls watch quietly,
>
> swallowing laughter,
>
> biting hope,
>
> hiding voices that ask why and how.



> Lessons are gone.
>
> Books gather dust.
>
> Pencils sit untouched,
>
> waiting for hands that will never hold them.



> Outside, children run and shout,
>
> but girls stand behind gates,
>
> their eyes on the ground,
>
> steps slow, heavy, careful.



> Education is a ghost,
>
> taken before they could touch it,
>
> before they could dream it.



> They wrap themselves in cloth,
>
> silent soldiers of survival,
>
> hiding smiles,
>
> hiding questions,
>
> hiding futures no one promised.



> Snow falls on the empty streets,
>
> rain falls on bare feet,
>
> and still, they walk,
>
> carrying hunger in their stomachs,
>
> fear in their hearts,
>
> and courage they cannot name.



> One girl whispers in her mind:
>
> Bread, pen, school… one day they will be mine.



> But the world is loud and deaf,
>
> walls do not listen,
>
> doors do not open.



> Mothers whisper:
>
> Be patient, my child.
>
> Daughters ask:
>
> For how long?



> And silence answers,
>
> bitter and heavy,
>
> like shadows on their skin.



> At night, they sit on cold floors,
>
> books untouched,
>
> shelves lined with dust,
>
> dreams stacked like stones
>
> they dare not move.



> But still, their eyes shine,
>
> like candles
>
> the wind cannot snuff out.



> And still, their hearts beat,
>
> small but steady,
>
> with a quiet hope
>
> that someday,
>
> someone will let them read,
>
> someone will let them write,
>
> someone will let them live.



> They learn patience,
>
> they learn endurance,
>
> they learn silence,
>
> but never surrender.



> And in the darkness,
>
> their small light waits,
>
> a whisper that refuses to die:
>
> We will rise.
>
> We will learn.
>
> We will live.

stories.title: The Winter That Never Smiled
stories.description: Set against the wounded silence of Kabul and the destroyed Buddha of Bamyan, this story recounts the author’s grief, exile, and the tragic loss of a friend taken and broken by oppression. Through memory and promise, it becomes an act of witnessing and remembrance.
stories.authorBio: I am S.R., a woman writing to give voice to Afghan women and remind others of the power of hope and resilience.
stories.content:
It was a cold, dry winter. Buda, with his wounded body, still watched over the city,  
silent and steadfast. After work, I always took the path past him to reach my home.  
There were shorter routes, but I chose that one just to see him. It felt like visiting an  
old friend.

In Buda’s wounds, I saw my own. He had been targeted for standing firm, for bearing  
witness to history, for representing a culture and knowledge long silenced.

In the days that followed, it felt as if Buda had lowered his head under the weight of  
the world. Every time I passed him, I could not meet his gaze; I lowered mine too,  
carrying a portion of his sorrow. The air seemed heavier, the streets quieter, and the  
shadows longer. This was not what we had earned, not what we had fought for. We  
had grown up believing in laughter, in festivals, in sunlight on the mountains and yet  
here we were, walking past a silent witness to our loss, our hearts pressed down under  
the weight of fear and grief.

For a few minutes, I stared at him, my chest tight. I had been forced to leave Kabul  
after the Taliban took over. Fear followed us like a shadow, the nightmares of the  
previous generation returning. The world seemed to have forgotten us. In the corners  
of the city, bodies appeared, nameless and unattended, and no one claimed  
responsibility for their deaths.

I loved Bamyan, the Potato Flower Festival, the Dambura music, the laughter of  
people in Band-e Amir, but now, fear had taken root behind the eyes of children, and  
in the gaze of the girls, I saw something like exhaustion and despair, far older than  
their years.

Then I received a message.  
"Zahra is gone."

I could not believe it. Zahra, with her deep laugh that could fill a room, her strength  
and kindness, how could she no longer be here?

Our phone lines were not safe. I contacted another friend online. Her voice trembled  
as she spoke. Zahra had been taken from her home days before by the Taliban,  
accused of actions they deemed unacceptable. Her family searched frantically, going  
from office to office, but all were denied access. After six days, the Taliban confirmed  
they had her, and demanded her father pay 250,000 Afghanis as a fine. They also  
forced a written promise that Zahra would not repeat the acts they condemned.

When Zahra finally returned home, she was not the same girl. Her mother watched  
her closely, noticing every hesitation, every silence. The light in her eyes had dimmed,  
the warmth in her smile was gone, and her movements carried a heaviness that had  
not been there before. The girl who had left was fractured, carrying the weight of  
what she had endured. When her mother asked her what had happened, Zahra would  
only whisper,  
"I am tired. I need to rest."

The quiet in her room was heavier than any words. Her suffering was visible in the  
way she moved, the way she avoided gaze, and the heaviness in her breath. The light  
in her eyes, so full of hope before, had dimmed.

And then she was gone. Zahra had taken her own life, her story carried with her.  
I could not bring myself to attend her funeral. I was not brave enough to say goodbye.  
I wept for a long time, and as the cold, sorrowful sun sank behind the mountains, I  
stood before Buda and made a promise: I would tell her story. Now, my tears no  
longer hold me back. I write for her, and for all those like her, hoping that even a  
single reader might glimpse how we live here, the fear, the loss, and the quiet courage  
that endures despite it all.

stories.title: Through the Lens - The Day I Spoke to a Leaf
stories.description: A young girl’s first encounter with a microscope in her school library becomes a life‑changing moment. Seeing the hidden beauty of a leaf awakens her passion for science and medicine, creating a spark that continues to guide her even after her education and opportunities are taken away.
stories.authorBio: Nilab Mohammadi is a young woman from Mazar-e-Sharif, Afghanistan, who was a medical student before the country's collapse interrupted her studies; now, she volunteers as an online English teacher, supports Afghan girls deprived of education, and uses writing to empower women and inspire hope.
stories.content:
Tomorrow is Tuesday, and I have science class. Yes, SCIENCE.

I couldn’t contain my excitement. The butterflies in my stomach had turned into birds, beating their wings wildly. For two weeks, we had only read about the unseen world of science, but tomorrow, we would finally see it. A real microscope, donated by UNICEF, was coming to our school—the first technological device we had ever owned. It felt like science fiction.

“Mom, can I wear my school uniform tonight?” I asked quietly, full of hope.

She sighed and said, “I will wake you up early, so don’t wear your uniform to bed.” She seemed a bit irritated—who wouldn’t be after being asked the same question fourteen times, perhaps nineteen, as she argued.

I had spent days imagining what it would feel like to see the tiny vascular system of a leaf. Still, waiting was unavoidable. What if someone breaks it? I worried about myself. Then I reassured myself just as quickly, No, no, don’t be ridiculous, Nilab. Mrs. Sadat would never allow that. Yet the fear lingered.

Tuesday, 5:30 a.m.

I woke up before the sun. The morning air was cold, but excitement carried me forward. I performed my morning prayer, asking the Lord to protect the device and allow me to see through the lens. I rushed out so fast that I didn’t hear my mother calling my name for her sweet halwa breakfast or my father laughing at my impatience. Somehow, I made it to our dusty school library. And there it was!

The microscope sat quietly on the table—gray, with a scratched base. I didn’t care. To me, it looked like a portal. For a moment, it felt as if the famous Professor Proton from a science fiction show had stepped into our classroom.

“How does this device make tiny veins appear so large?” I asked, unable to hide my excitement.

“Hold your horses, Nilab. You will see,” Mrs. Sadat replied with a knowing smile.

She placed a thin glass slide onto the stage and gently laid a small leaf on it. Her focus was so intense it felt like surgery.

“Go for it,” she said.

I pointed to myself.

“Me?”

“Yes, you,” Mrs. Sadat replied with a smile.

I couldn’t reach the table easily—my height was too short—so I raised myself onto my toes to be a bit taller. When I lowered my eye to the lens, the world disappeared.

A simple leaf transformed into a galaxy of minute bridges—veins branching like rivers, cells forming intricate, city-like patterns. I was afraid to blink, worried the labyrinth might vanish. But it didn’t.

I forgot the stale, metallic smell of the library. I didn’t hear my teacher asking me to let the next student look. I was completely hooked.

That small leaf, picked from the school garden, became more than a specimen. It became a mentor, guiding me along my path. That early spark created a road toward medical school—the path to becoming a doctor, someone who finds cures and brings hope.

Later, my school was taken away. The microscope was taken from my hands. The university and its classes were taken too.

Still, I will remember that moment forever, the moment I found my spark. It was the first time I truly saw the different patterns of life: delicate, fragile, yet astonishing.

The microscope is no longer in my hands; it lives in my soul, acting like a lantern—lighting my path and urging me to move forward.

stories.title: Where Hope Becomes Action
stories.description: This story shares the journey of an Afghan girl who faced displacement, fear, and loss of education as a refugee in Pakistan and later upon returning to Afghanistan. Despite restrictions and hardship, she continued learning, developed her talents, found leadership through EmpowerHer, and remained committed to education, justice, and hope for Afghan girls.
stories.authorBio: Mahtab Ebrahimi is a 12th grade online student in Kabul, English teacher, graphic designer, and advocate for Afghan girls' education and empowerment, with work published by the Malala Fund.
stories.content:
My story begins when we immigrated to Pakistan in 2022. Living as a displaced refugee was very challenging there, as we could not afford to extend our visas, and I was completely hopeless about my future. I wasn’t able to attend a regular school because of documentation, and financial issues were piling up at their greatest. But I realized these kinds of challenges should not stop me from dreaming. So I started online learning, joined English and Graphic Designing courses offered by UNHCR in Pakistan. I also started singing and performing national anthems at events, where my team and I were awarded by Afghan and Pakistani organizations many times. Besides that, I started teaching English in a small refugee academy. I was pursuing my goals and dreaming of a peaceful future. My life wasn’t perfect in Pakistan, but at least I was able to continue my education—the hope that moved me forward.

However, the deportation of Afghan refugees started in 2025 by the Pakistani government. This prevented me from my work and attending classes in academies. We were in constant fear of being deported. Those were truly terrifying days for me because I did not want to go back to Afghanistan. But fate had different plans for us. The situation was getting worse day by day, and eventually we were forced to come back. It was really hard to put all your efforts there and come back to zero—where education is banned and voices are silenced. I was sad and disappointed about coming back here because I do not see any future for myself, nor for my family.

After a while, I witnessed how Afghan girls in Kabul were trying their best and standing against the oppressive policies. That really sparked hope in me. It motivated me—if we survived under these conditions and still go for our biggest dreams and push our limits, what else is there to fear? The answer is: NOTHING. There’s nothing else for us to fear, and that’s why we are unstoppable and resilient no matter what we face!

I gained hope and motivation and continued my online school. Furthermore, I applied to as many opportunities as possible and started chasing my dreams once again. During that time, I came across EmpowerHer and was accepted into the Leadership and Personal Development Workshop. From the beginning of the workshop, it felt truly incredible, because not all online classes paid enough attention to the students. But EmpowerHer is different. It is a safe space for me where I am able to share my thoughts and opinions openly, without any judgement and without limitations regarding my age or knowledge level. At EmpowerHer, I saw in the speech of my classmates and mentors the desire to bring a positive change in society. It was a truly amazing workshop and I learned about self-leadership and leadership at local and global stages. I learned to take matters into my own hands. I learned to listen to others and ask for their guidance with confidence.

Through every loss and new beginning, I learned that leadership is not about positions, but about actions. Even when schools were closed and we were denied our rights and opportunities, I created my own path through learning, raising my voice, and going beyond limits. My journey is still continuing, but I carry one promise with me: no matter where life takes me, I will keep working for education and justice for Afghan girls.

My final words for Afghan girls are to dream as big as you can, even when the world tries to limit you. Remember that your strength, courage, and voice matter.

Let's keep learning, keep rising, and keep supporting each other. Together we will build a brighter future for ourselves and Afghanistan.

stories.title: Empowering Woman
stories.description: This blog emphasizes that women’s empowerment is essential for a just and thriving world. When women have equal rights, education, and opportunities, entire communities benefit. It highlights the struggle of Afghan girls denied schooling and calls for global solidarity to ensure every girl can learn, dream, and shape her future. Empowering women uplifts families, strengthens nations, and keeps the world’s light from fading.
stories.authorBio: My name is Faryal Asadzai, and I am a young writer who expresses herself through poetry and storytelling. I blend imagination with honest feelings in everything I write. And I am excited to share my voice with the world.
stories.content:
Imagine growing up knowing you have dreams, but also knowing the world may never let you chase them simply because of your gender. For millions of women, this is not imagination, it is daily reality.

Imagine a world where half the stars suddenly went dark. What would happen? That world would feel incomplete, unbalanced, and unable to shine the way it was meant to. This is exactly what happens when women are held back from reaching their full potential.

For centuries, women around the world have carried families, communities, and entire cultures on their shoulders, yet their voices have often been silenced, and their abilities underestimated. Today, as the world faces complex challenges, empowering women is a necessity.

Women’s empowerment means giving women the freedom, opportunities, and respect they need to make decisions about their own lives. It includes access to education, the right to work, equal treatment, and the ability to participate fully in society. In many places, progress has been made, but millions of women still face barriers that limit their dreams.

Understanding why women’s empowerment matters is essential not just for women themselves, but for families, communities, and nations. Communities grow when women are allowed to learn and participate. Education opens opportunities, gives women awareness of their rights, and protects them from exploitation.

Without education, women face limited choices, fewer job opportunities, and a higher risk of being controlled by others. But when women study, they gain confidence and the tools to support themselves and their families.

Countries with low female education rates often struggle with poverty, poor healthcare, and weak social systems. In contrast, when women are educated, they become lawyers, teachers, leaders, and business owners who contribute directly to the community.

For example, in Rwanda, after the government increased girls’ education, more women joined schools, businesses, and politics, which helped the country grow faster and improve healthcare and education for everyone.

This proves that empowering women is not just a “women’s issue”; it is a community development way that improves the quality of life for everyone.

Sometimes the simplest questions shakes us the most. Why, in a world full of discoveries, solutions, and possibilities, are millions of women still told they cannot study, cannot work, cannot choose, cannot dream? In Afghanistan today, girls are banned from secondary schools and universities. Sisters watch their brothers leave for class while they sit at home, waiting for a future that feels like it’s disappearing. This isn’t just a tragedy for those girls; it’s a reminder of how much the world still struggles with recognizing women as equal human beings.

Empowering women begins with something simple yet powerful: giving them the same rights, opportunities, and respect that men receive by default. When women receive education, they don’t just transform their own lives; they change the course of entire communities. When girls are educated, child marriage rates drop, health improves, and future generations become more capable. Beyond this, the empowerment of women means allowing every girl to imagine herself as someone who matters, capable of shaping her own life.

The denial of this basic right, like in Afghanistan, where girls are locked out of schools, shows how dangerous it is when society fears educated women. Empowerment is not only about school or degrees; it’s about giving women the freedom to make decisions about their own lives.

Educated women often raise children who are healthier, more confident, and more likely to go to school. And by this each generation becomes better than the last.

For example, imagine a girl who is allowed to study and grows up to become a trained nurse. Her knowledge doesn’t just end at her job; she brings it home, teaching her family about hygiene, nutrition, and proper medical care. Her children grow up stronger, her household becomes safer, and her community benefits. Additionally, women who earn their own income spend it on food, education, and household needs. Every step forward that a woman takes spreads to her family, her community, and eventually the entire country.

Another reason empowering women matters is that societies cannot be fair or successful when half the population is silenced. For centuries, women have been excluded from leadership roles and major decisions, even though their perspectives are necessary.

When women are part of shaping laws, communities, and policies, decisions become more balanced and thoughtful. Countries with more women in government often have stronger protections for children and better educational systems. Without their voices, important issues like safety, education, and health are often ignored or handled poorly.

Empowering women ensures that every individual has a chance to influence the future, not just those who have traditionally held power.

But empowerment isn’t only about education and economics; it is also about dignity, safety, and the freedom to choose. Millions of women face violence, harassment, and discrimination simply for existing in public spaces. In some cultures, women are taught to shrink themselves, to speak softly, to lower their eyes, to carry fear as part of their identity.

Imagine the weight of living like that. Empowerment means breaking these invisible chains. It means teaching girls that their worth is not measured by obedience or silence, but by their courage, ambition, and humanity. When women feel safe and respected, societies become kinder, more just, and more compassionate. Their perspectives bring balance and empathy to decision-making processes that shape the future.

Empowering women matters because without it, the world will never move forward. When women are silenced, a country loses half of its strength, half of its ideas, and half of its future. We see this clearly in Afghanistan, where girls with dreams as big as the sky are kept from school, not because they lack talent, but because they lack the freedom to use it. Yet even when their classrooms are taken away, their hope never disappears.

Afghan girls continue to believe in a future where they can study, choose, and become whoever they want to be. Their courage reminds us that empowerment doesn’t come from silence; it comes from raising our voices, standing together, and refusing to give up. When women rise, everyone rises.

And as long as there are girls fighting for their rights, we must stand beside them, speak for them, and make sure the world sees their worth. A society becomes stronger, kinder, and more just when every woman is allowed to live with dignity, opportunity, and dreams.

That is why we must keep pushing, keep speaking, and keep fighting for a world where every girl, no matter where she is born, can finally step into the life she deserves.

So lets always remember to give women their rights, speak up for them and stand with them. And please, lets not forget the brave girls in Afghanistan whose dreams are on pause, the girls who deserve the same freedom, the same voice, and the same chance to shine.

stories.title: My Voice from the Heart of Darkness
stories.description: This blog recounts the inspiring journey of a young Afghan girl who, after the Taliban disrupts her education, finds resilience through online learning. Forced into tailoring, she ultimately reclaims her identity and confidence, becoming an 11th-grade student in an American online school. Proudly identifying as a builder rather than just a survivor, she dreams of studying computer science and advocates for the voices of Afghan girls, embodying the enduring light of hope in the darkest circumstances.
stories.authorBio: Nazanin Razawi is a dedicated writer, author, and passionate advocate for girls' education in Afghanistan. With a strong background in writing articles, essays, and letters that address critical social issues, she strives to inspire change and empower women through her work. Her dream is to establish an organization that provides unrestricted access to education for girls in underserved communities. Nazanin is committed to using her abilities in writing, communication, and leadership to help create a brighter and more equitable future for the next generation.
stories.content:
In the heart of darkness if there is a light, that's from us.

There were some nights that Kabul became silent than anytime. As if the city shut in its breath to scare less from the shadows of the persons that were passing through the alleys. I was a girl on those nights with eyes full of questions and a traumatic heart from the days that everything turned upside down.
The day that the sky of my country collapsed and my life was divided into two parts: before the fall and after that.

In the republic era I was an intelligent student. A girl who loves to learn; always with books, curiosity, and with big dreams.
